newsitem.title: UK: MID-OCTOBER AIR CARGO EXPORTS AT HIGHEST LEVELS SEEN THIS YEAR.
newsitem.headline: MID-OCTOBER AIR CARGO EXPORTS AT HIGHEST LEVELS SEEN THIS YEAR.

text.p: Mid-October air cargo exports from the UK are at highest levels seen so far this year driven by both seasonal factors and strong demand, with rates hardening although few formal tariff increases have been seen, a Reuters survey shows.

"Firming yields, rather than just raising prices, remains the aim at the moment," said one source. Pressures on fuel prices are not seen as an immediate threat to rates, but a surcharge cannot be ruled out, he added.
Demand is strong for cargo capacity on virtually all routes, while a number of carriers especially to the Far East, said they are turning away business.
And the first time in 1996, there are also clear signs of the long-awaited recovery in westbound transatlantic traffic with volumes rising and capacity declining, the survey shows.

Roger Blacklock of the British International Freight Association (BIFA) said the latest available data suggests overall air cargo exports were up three percent from the start of the year by August/September, with growth to the U.S up nine percent.
Rates to Tokyo are around 2.05 stg a kg compared with 1.97 stg previously, while substantially higher rates are available on some direct carriers.
Seoul is around 1.95 stg compared to the previous 1.85 with. Hong Kong is marginally firmer at 1.20 stg.

"Business to Japan is very good," with October continuing the strong trend seen in September, said Japan Airline's Tony Edwards. "The forecast for the next month and the next six months should be pretty good," he added.
At All Nippon Airways," Business in buoyant and we're looking at a record month in October for both tonnage and revenue," since the service started in 1989, an ANA cargo source said.
The two airlines are moving respectively 150 tonnes and 250 tonnes a week of cargo to Japan.
Korean Airlines is planning a five pence a kg increase in its general rates from November 1, to 2.05 stg a kg for 100 kg, said the carrier's cargo manager, Frank Smith.
The rise comes against a background of strong two-way trade between the UK and Korea.
Meanwhile Philippine Airlines which moved to Heathrow from Gatwick has been turning away to due lack of cargo uplift capacity on its new non-stop London-Manila McDonnell Douglas MD-11 flight.
When Airbus 340-300s are introduced on October 26, capacity is expected to be between five to 12 tonnes depending on the exact route being flown, said PAL's cargo manager, Keith O'Callaghan.
